claims.proposition_evaluated: The City's latest published condition ratings available by 2026-09-03 show that its Roads asset class was in poor condition as of the inventory date described by those ratings.
claims.interpretation_notes: Partially supported under the primary and alternative cutoffs. The 2025 report's Roads class has 11.2% rated D or F by replacement value, above 10% but below 25%. Its nested classes are Paved Roads (12.5% D/F), Unpaved Roads (100% not rated) and Curbs (7.0%). The class total is the verdict-bearing measure; dropping curbs or combining classes differently would create a category the City does not publish. The report describes the inventory as of December 31, 2024, not conditions during the August–September 2026 capture period. The City publishes A/B and D/F combined, so separate A, B, D and F shares are unavailable. I found no City-published length-based Roads distribution or current Roads D/F target in the evidence reviewed.

supporting_evidence.finding: Appendix B reports the City-named Roads class at 70.8% Good (A/B), 16.2% Fair (C), 11.2% Poor (D/F), and 1.7% Not Rated by replacement value. Nested rows are Paved Roads (12.5% D/F), Unpaved Roads (100% not rated), and Curbs (7.0% D/F).

The required catalogue and report-material search for a separate current alley condition rating was not completed here, so I cannot conclude from an access or search failure that no such measure exists.

claims.proposition_evaluated: At least half of the C$100 million Council approved for CM-20-0330 came from funding sources that permitted road or alley renewal instead.
claims.interpretation_notes: Supported under both cutoff sets. The adopted profile sheet assigns all C$100 million to Tax-Supported Debt. Under the brief's fixed rule, general municipal capital funding of this kind is eligible unless the record establishes a restriction. The later project-specific borrowing authorization and subsequent C$430,000 reduction from CM-20-0330 do not change the source breakdown of the original approval or establish that Council could not have allocated general tax-supported debt to renewal when it made that budget choice. This finding addresses source eligibility, not what Council would have approved in a counterfactual or whether a later transfer occurred.

supporting_evidence.finding: The adopted CM-20-0330 profile identifies Tax-Supported Debt as the sole approved funding source: C$5.950 million in 2023, C$26.750 million in 2024, C$33.650 million in 2025 and C$33.650 million in 2026, totalling C$100.000 million. The profile table prints in thousands.
supporting_evidence.source_title: Adopted 2023–2026 Capital Budget, CM-20-0330 profile, pp. 540–543
supporting_evidence.establishes: The amount and identified source for every dollar of the original approved profile; under the brief's eligibility rule, E is C$100.0 million, X is zero and U is zero.

supporting_evidence.finding: Council's December 2022 post-meeting record documents the budget deliberations and approval of the profile.
supporting_evidence.source_title: City Council - Budget - November 30, 2022, post-meeting minutes
supporting_evidence.establishes: The Council approval record; the adopted profile sheet supplies the detailed funding-source amounts.

challenging_evidence.finding: A later borrowing bylaw authorized debt for the specified active-transportation project. That later authorization governs the approved borrowing and does not establish that Council could not have allocated general tax-supported debt to road or alley renewal when adopting the budget.
challenging_evidence.establishes: A later project-specific borrowing authorization that qualifies how the approved funds could be used after authorization, without negating the original budget source eligibility.

challenging_evidence.finding: A June 2025 adjustment reduced CM-20-0330 by C$430,000 for a stated active-transportation connection purpose in Dunluce. The source record does not establish a transfer from renewal funding into CM-20-0330.
challenging_evidence.source_title: Spring 2025 Supplemental Capital Budget Adjustment, Attachment 4, item 4.1-1; Bylaw 21265 report
challenging_evidence.establishes: A later change in the opposite direction and the need to keep source eligibility distinct from a transfer calculation.

limitations: The profile identifies the general funding source, but this finding does not establish that Council would have approved an additional road or alley renewal project, that debt servicing had no cost, or that the approved borrowing could later be redirected without Council action.

A complete transaction-by-transaction reconciliation of December 2022 deliberations and all capital budget adjustments through 2026-09-03 was not established by the evidence reviewed. The reported C$430,000 transfer out should not be described as a transfer from renewal funding without a record identifying the affected renewal allocation.

The required list of every December 2022 motion, its mover, amount and disposition, every adjustment through the as-of date, the renewal-funded transfer total in both directions, and CM-20-0330 actual expenditures for 2023–2025 remains incomplete.
unknowns: Whether a complete adjustment ledger identifies any transfer from a renewal-funded portion into CM-20-0330 before the as-of date.
The complete motion-by-motion record and year-end actual expenditure arithmetic required by the brief.

claims.proposition_evaluated: The C$100 million approved for bike lanes equalled a serious share of the infrastructure renewal shortfall Edmonton itself reports.
claims.interpretation_notes: Partially supported under the primary and alternative cutoffs. The adopted 2023–2026 Capital Budget explicitly calls the C$1.63 billion difference a “renewal funding gap” for 2023–2026. C$100 million divided by C$1.63 billion is approximately 6.13%, above the 5% floor and below the 25% primary serious-share threshold. Other reviewers surfaced a later City-reported amount of approximately C$1.52 billion for the same cycle; that gives approximately 6.58% and the same classification. The adopted budget's exact published pair is C$3,575.584 million ideal investment and C$1,945.673 million funded RIMS ideal investment. The C$2,194.927 million total funded renewal line is broader and is not substituted into that gap calculation. This is a capital-to-capital comparison for matching years.

supporting_evidence.finding: The City's adopted budget says ideal renewal investment was C$3.58 billion and funding available to renewal was C$1.95 billion, and calls the difference a C$1.63 billion “renewal funding gap” for 2023–2026. Table 6 gives C$3,575.584 million in RIMS Ideal Investment and C$1,945.673 million in Funded RIMS Ideal Investment.
supporting_evidence.source_title: Adopted 2023–2026 Capital Budget, Renewal discussion and Tables 5–6, pp. 47–49
supporting_evidence.establishes: A City-published same-period shortfall and its own wording; C$100 million / C$1.63 billion is about 6.13%.
supporting_evidence.quote: the City has a renewal funding gap of $1.63 billion for 2023-2026

supporting_evidence.finding: The City’s 2024 Financial Annual Report was reported to give an approximately C$1.52 billion 2023–2026 renewal investment shortfall; a later Fall 2025 City budget presentation repeated a C$1.52 billion 2023–2026 Capital Budget Renewal Funding Gap.
supporting_evidence.source_title: City of Edmonton 2024 Financial Annual Report, Asset Renewal Investment
supporting_evidence.establishes: A later same-period City-reported gap amount surfaced in the round-1 evidence; using it gives about 6.58% and does not change the classification.

challenging_evidence.finding: The adopted budget's C$1.63 billion gap is much larger than C$100 million: the ratio is about 6.13%, below the 25% threshold for Supported.
challenging_evidence.source_title: Adopted 2023–2026 Capital Budget, Renewal discussion, pp. 48–49
challenging_evidence.establishes: The proposition's “serious share” threshold is not met on the City's published same-period gap.

challenging_evidence.finding: The budget distinguishes C$2,194.927 million total funded renewal from C$1,945.673 million of the modelled ideal investment funded. Its gap calculation uses the latter and excludes specified pre-commitments and other additional items.
challenging_evidence.establishes: The denominator must follow the City's stated gap basis rather than substitute the broader total funded renewal amount.

limitations: The approximately C$1.52 billion later figure was surfaced in other reviewers' findings, but its underlying Fall 2025 presentation was not independently opened in this review. The directly verified adopted-budget figure is C$1.63 billion; both yield Partially supported.
No City-published 2023–2026 roads-and-alleys shortfall, unit cost for renewal output, or benchmark for the share of renewal requirement funded was verified here.
